source.title: Mitigating Deep Double Descent by Concatenating Inputs
source.authors: John Chen; Qihan Wang; Anastasios Kyrillidis

record.tranche_reason: The authors explicitly reproduce settings from prior double-descent studies and measure test error across model sizes, training epochs, and sample counts; they also test an input-concatenation construction in those settings.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own linear-regression sample-count sweep and deep-network model-size and epoch sweeps. The bias-variance decomposition is also a reported measurement. Cited results from other papers are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper reproduces Belkin et al. (MNIST one-hidden-layer), Nakkiran et al. (ResNet18 width and epoch sweeps), Nakkiran 2019 (linear sample-wise) and Yang et al. (bias-variance). It reports its own curves for the standard settings and for a concatenated-input dataset construction.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors also state the construction 'generally mitigates' double descent without causing underfitting. They suggest it may act as implicit regularization for small models, and that the links between samples, parameters and capacity need rethinking.
record.recipe_differences: The paper reproduces prior linear-regression and deep-network settings, then adds a dataset construction that stacks pairs of inputs and combines their targets. It varies model width and training duration in the deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome varies with input construction: self-concatenating each MNIST input leaves double descent nearly unchanged, while concatenating different inputs removes it; on CIFAR, concatenation mitigates model-size and epoch-wise curves, with reported differences between CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.

fits_no_version.finding: Artificially multiplying the sample count by concatenating input pairs, with little new information, mitigates or removes the deep-network peak. The same construction leaves the linear-regression peak unchanged.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In deep networks, the interpolation peak depends on how a 'sample' is constructed, not only on the raw sample count relative to parameters.

record.peer_reviewed: Presented at the ICML 2021 Workshop on Overparameterization: Pitfalls & Opportunities
record.problems: Most deep-network curve results are described qualitatively or presented in figures without numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The sample-count experiment is linear regression; the deep-network sample manipulation is artificial input concatenation rather than a sweep over the number of original training examples.

untested.parts: Architectures other than a one-hidden-layer MLP, ResNet18 and ResNet-34. Label-noise settings. Numeric peak heights are not reported.
The standard CIFAR-100 epoch-wise curve, which is shown in a figure only. Other architectures and optimizers.
Sample-wise non-monotonicity in deep networks. Only linear ridgeless regression is swept over real sample count.
Label-noise dependence, multiple or triple peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.

missing.what: MNIST test-error curves (Fig. 2 bottom row) are not described in the text. Rows R1–R3 record loss.
Bias curves in the ResNet-34 decomposition are plotted but not recorded.

record.verdict_notes: This is a workshop paper. All deep-network results are qualitative, from figures, with no seeds or uncertainty reported. The concatenated-input conditions are a data manipulation, so verdicts on them are scope limits, not challenges to the natural-setting effect.

versions.untested_parts: The experiments cover MNIST one-hidden-layer networks and ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100; they do not establish the behavior for all deep networks or settings.
Epoch-wise results are reported for ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, not for all model classes or training regimes.
The sample-count sweep is the min-norm ridgeless linear-regression setting. The paper does not sweep the number of original training samples in its deep-network experiments.
No systematic capacity sweep across model classes testing whether the general curve subsumes the classical U-shaped curve.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and samples.
The paper measures variance in one ResNet-34 setting, but does not test label-noise dependence, multiple or triple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
The paper does not recalculate complexity using an effective number of parameters or test whether that produces an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: min-norm ridgeless regression
rows.operation_detail: Vary the number of samples before any concatenation.

rows.operation_detail: Apply the concatenated-input construction to the linear-regression sample-count setting.
rows.measure: test MSE versus number of samples
rows.value: The concatenated construction does not affect the double-descent curve; the peak occurs in the exact same location.
rows.note: The authors say the construction does not add information in this linear-regression setting.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Decompose error into bias and variance across five splits of 10,000 training samples.
rows.value: The paper describes a significantly sharper unimodal variance curve than in the concatenated-input condition.
rows.note: This is a variance measurement relevant to the proposed variance account.
rows.check: This is a variance curve, not test error, so it does not bear on V1. The sharp unimodal variance in the standard case bears on the variance account in V6.

rows.subject: ResNet-34
rows.operation_detail: Decompose error into bias and variance across five splits of 10,000 training samples.
rows.value: The concatenated construction significantly delays and smoothens the increase in variance relative to the standard case.
rows.note: The authors suggest this may reflect implicit regularization for small models.
rows.check: This is a variance measure, not test error, so it does not bear on V1. Delayed and smoother variance accompanies a shifted test-error bump.

rows.subject: ResNet-34

conditions.value: concatenated inputs compared with standard case

rows.value: The text reports a shifted bump in test error for the concatenated-input construction.
rows.note: The paper relates the changed test-error shape to the altered variance curve.
rows.check: The row merges two conditions: the standard case (bump present, observed) and the concatenated case (shifted bump, partial). It should be split into two rows.

source_check.correct: Concatenated-input ResNet-34 retains a test-error bump at a shifted width. Its V1 state is observed rather than partial on the stated evidence; a shift alone does not establish attenuation. Record the standard condition separately if using it as an independent supporting result.
source_check.problem: The text reports displacement of a persistent bump, without establishing that the double-descent effect is incomplete or weaker.

statements.correction: This study: ResNet18; CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100; 1000 training epochs; standard CIFAR-10 medium models show a U shape and larger models show double descent; measure is test error; own-experiment label-noise rate is not stated; no VGG experiment is reported.
statements.problem: R9 supports qualitative epoch-wise double descent for larger ResNet18s, but the surrounding description does not identify this study's setting and could attribute noisy-label, VGG or expected zero-one-loss experiments to it.
